ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Participants are 156 people surveyed from one mixed-security women's correctional facility in the Midwest.

> Participants were recruited through a larger parent research project related to mental health screening or through a trauma treatment research study.

> Ninety out of 156 participants were recruited through screening for a trauma treatment study.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Conventional mental health treatments may not translate to carceral settings.
A clearer understanding of the experiences and preferences of incarcerated individuals is needed.
Based on literature and expertise from community partners, this project surveyed individuals at a women's prison about their treatment preferences.
Results showed high favorability for mental health treatment across the board, with the highest ratings for self-administered options.
Participants also preferred Department of Corrections providers over peers and individual support over group.

Clinical considerations for treatment for incarcerated women are discussed including prioritizing confidentiality, investing in self-administered options, incorporating individualized elements into group programming, and using preference surveys to inform resource allocation.
Rates of most mental illnesses are higher in the incarcerated population than in the general population (Prins, 2014).
text.formatted: Rates of most mental illnesses are higher in the incarcerated population than in the general population <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Prins, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Rates of mental illness are particularly high in incarcerated women, with three out of four struggling with mental health (James and Glaze, 2006), half meeting criteria for PTSD during their lifetime (Baranyi et al., 2018), and the majority with a history of a substance use disorder (National Institute on Drug Abuse, 2020).
text.formatted: Rates of mental illness are particularly high in incarcerated women, with three out of four struggling with mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(James and Glaze, 2006)</ref>, half meeting criteria for PTSD during their lifetime <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baranyi et al., 2018)</ref>, and the majority with a history of a substance use disorder (National Institute on Drug Abuse, 2020).

text.text: Women are the fastest growing incarcerated demographic in the United States (Monazzam and Budd, 2023).
text.formatted: Women are the fastest growing incarcerated demographic in the United States <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Monazzam and Budd, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Specific care and consideration towards providing feasible, acceptable, and effective mental health interventions for incarcerated women is essential.

However, research on mental healthcare for incarcerated women shows small effects for reductions in depressive, anxiety, and PTSD symptomatology, inconclusive long-term impacts, and a lack of high-quality controlled intervention studies (Bartlett et al., 2015; Malik et al., 2021; Yoon et al., 2017).
text.formatted: However, research on mental healthcare for incarcerated women shows small effects for reductions in depressive, anxiety, and PTSD symptomatology, inconclusive long-term impacts, and a lack of high-quality controlled intervention studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bartlett et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Malik et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Yoon et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The American Psychological Association defines Evidence-Based Practice (EBP) in psychology as "the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences" (APA Presidental Task Force on Evidence-Based Practice, 2006, p. 278).
text.formatted: The American Psychological Association defines Evidence-Based Practice (EBP) in psychology as "the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences" (APA Presidental Task Force on <ref type="bibr">Evidence-Based Practice, 2006, p. 278)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, patient preference has been known to be a key factor in therapeutic care for almost two decades.
Meta-analyses show that clients matched to their treatment preference show larger reductions in symptomatology (Delevry and Le, 2019; Lindhiem et al., 2014; Swift and Callahan, 2009).
text.formatted: Meta-analyses show that clients matched to their treatment preference show larger reductions in symptomatology (Delevry and Le, 2019; <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Lindhiem et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Swift and Callahan, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Patients who have treatment matched to preference and/or are involved in the treatment decision process also endorse a stronger therapeutic alliance, report greater treatment satisfaction, and have lower attrition rates (Lindhiem et al., 2014; Swift and Callahan, 2009; Windle et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Patients who have treatment matched to preference and/or are involved in the treatment decision process also endorse a stronger therapeutic alliance, report greater treatment satisfaction, and have lower attrition rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lindhiem et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Swift and Callahan, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Windle et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, the implementation of treatment approaches that are consistent with preferences of incarcerated women could bolster effectiveness.

Upon review of the literature of types of treatments, treatment providers, and treatment modalities offered in carceral settings, we discussed treatment options with our DOC partners, and the options discussed below were deemed feasible.
Two common providers of mental health services during incarceration are clinicians and peers.
An incarcerated person may prefer a clinician if they feel safer with someone who has extensive training.
However, prison clinicians are often focused on crisis management and may have limited time for building therapeutic relationships (Fazel et al., 2017; Hawton et al., 2014).
text.formatted: However, prison clinicians are often focused on crisis management and may have limited time for building therapeutic relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fazel et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hawton et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Another option is peer support.

A metaanalysis on the effects of peer support for mental illness in the community found no support for a reduction in psychiatric symptoms, but did find evidence of increased self-reported views of recovery and empowerment (White et al., 2020).
text.formatted: A metaanalysis on the effects of peer support for mental illness in the community found no support for a reduction in psychiatric symptoms, but did find evidence of increased self-reported views of recovery and empowerment <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(White et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Peer support in the prison setting can reduce conduct reports during incarceration and recidivism after release, as well as build self-awareness and purpose in peer providers (Bagnall et al., 2015; Kottke-Weaver, 2023).
text.formatted: Peer support in the prison setting can reduce conduct reports during incarceration and recidivism after release, as well as build self-awareness and purpose in peer providers <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bagnall et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Kottke-Weaver, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: No research with incarcerated women has investigated preference between facility staff and peer specialists for mental health treatment.

Both individual and group therapy can be beneficial for mental health and there are generally no clinically meaningful differences in outcomes between the two treatment approaches within community (Lockwood et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2005) or incarcerated samples (Yoon et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Both individual and group therapy can be beneficial for mental health and there are generally no clinically meaningful differences in outcomes between the two treatment approaches within community <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Lockwood et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ryan et al., 2005)</ref> or incarcerated samples <ref type="bibr">(Yoon et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Individual therapy provides an opportunity to target specific experiences, emotions, and core beliefs.
Individual therapy might be preferred by someone who struggles with vulnerability or asserting themselves in group settings.
Group therapy can provide community and an opportunity to connect.
Group therapy might be preferred by someone who wants to hear about others' experiences and appreciates space to listen.
Psychotropic medications are widely used in the correctional environment, particularly for women (Bentley and Casey, 2017; Hassan et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Psychotropic medications are widely used in the correctional environment, particularly for women <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bentley and Casey, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hassan et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Qualitative work with incarcerated women demonstrates complex views around psychotropic medication; many women endorse its benefits to maintain emotional stability, while others cite limited appointments with providers as a major barrier to managing side effects or lack of efficacy (Casey and Bentley, 2017; Hassan et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Qualitative work with incarcerated women demonstrates complex views around psychotropic medication; many women endorse its benefits to maintain emotional stability, while others cite limited appointments with providers as a major barrier to managing side effects or lack of efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Casey and Bentley, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hassan et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Given the ubiquity of medications and the mixed findings from qualitative studies, it is important to gain further clarity on preferences for this treatment option.
Self-administered support is one way to expand mental healthcare in prison at low cost.
Two feasible options are self-help workbooks and audio-based interventions.
Two studies that utilized self-help workbooks with incarcerated populations found decreases in anxiety (Maunder et al., 2009) and depression (Pardini et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Two studies that utilized self-help workbooks with incarcerated populations found decreases in anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Maunder et al., 2009)</ref> and depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Pardini et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: While there is no evidence yet on the effectiveness of an audio-based intervention in prison, mindfulness interventions have shown positive impacts for psychological wellbeing and behavioral functioning in this population and translate well to audio (Auty et al., 2017; Per et al., 2020).
text.formatted: While there is no evidence yet on the effectiveness of an audio-based intervention in prison, mindfulness interventions have shown positive impacts for psychological wellbeing and behavioral functioning in this population and translate well to audio <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Auty et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Per et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Self-administered options have multiple benefits for individuals receiving mental healthcare in prison.
Stigma surrounding mental illness is high in prison populations (Skogstad et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Stigma surrounding mental illness is high in prison populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Skogstad et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: A negative perception of those who experience mental health issues reduces the likelihood of treatment-seeking and treatment adherence (Corrigan, 2000; Farabee, Hall, Zaheer, and Joshi, 2019).
text.formatted: A negative perception of those who experience mental health issues reduces the likelihood of treatment-seeking and treatment adherence <ref type="bibr">(Corrigan, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Farabee, Hall, Zaheer, and Joshi, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The privacy of self-administered interventions could thus decrease hesitation to seek mental healthcare and increase retention.

In addition, research has shown that many incarcerated individuals are reluctant to receive mental healthcare from prison staff due to concerns about confidentiality and fear of consequences such as solitary confinement (Skogstad et al., 2005; Way et al., 2013).
text.formatted: In addition, research has shown that many incarcerated individuals are reluctant to receive mental healthcare from prison staff due to concerns about confidentiality and fear of consequences such as solitary confinement <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Skogstad et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Way et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: A self-administered option could provide access to mental health treatment for someone who would be unlikely to engage in treatment otherwise due to concerns around stigma and confidentiality.
Lastly, some individuals may not be ready for continuous treatment but are interested to learn more about mental health.

A one-day psychoeducation workshop to better understand the presentation of disorders such as anxiety, depression, and PTSD could begin the process of selfawareness for these individuals and may lead to future engagement with treatment.
Psychoeducation alone without treatment reduces depression and psychological distress (Donker et al., 2009) and increases mental health knowledge (Lincoln et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Psychoeducation alone without treatment reduces depression and psychological distress <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Donker et al., 2009)</ref> and increases mental health knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Lincoln et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: This option could allow for a large group of individuals to receive resources at one time.

While the need for more effective and acceptable mental healthcare within prison is clear, identifying the treatment preferences of individuals incarcerated at a women's correctional facility remains a missing piece to more impactful and widespread mental healthcare utilization.
There are four main study questions in service of this goal: 1) What are the mental health treatment preferences of incarcerated women?
2) How desired are self-administered treatment options?
3) Do treatment preferences vary by the provider of the service (prison therapist or peer) and the format of the support (individual or group)?
Does preference for individual or group options vary by provider?
4) How favorably do individuals rate treatment options overall?
Due to the relatively small literature on preferences of mental health treatment during incarceration, there are two hypotheses.

First, for question two, we hypothesize that selfadministered treatment options will be perceived favorably by incarcerated women considering potential distrust for prison staff, stigma around mental illness in incarcerated populations, and concerns around confidentiality and vulnerability in the prison setting.

Second, for question three, we hypothesize that incarcerated women will rate treatment from a prison therapist less favorably than treatment from a peer given prior evidence of distrust for prison staff.
Participants are 156 people surveyed from one mixed-security women's correctional facility in the Midwest.
Participants were recruited through a larger parent research project related to mental health screening or through a trauma treatment research study.
After considering past literature, we solicited input on the treatment options in our survey from our research partners at the state Department of Corrections (DOC).
Due to feedback from the DOC about the feasibility of virtual individual or group therapy, these two items were removed.
Community partners with lived experience of incarceration also reviewed the survey to provide feedback and were consulted to assist with interpreting the results of the study.
Above all, the survey was built to include choices that could be realistically implemented.

The final eight-question survey included the following options: 1) individual therapy with a DOC therapist, 2) group therapy with a DOC therapist, 3) individual support from a peer, 4) group support from a peer, 5) medication, 6) self-help workbook, 7) self-paced audio intervention, and 8) one-day psychoeducation workshop.
Participants rated how much they would like each treatment option on a Likert scale from "-2" (strongly dislike) to "2" (strongly like).
A score of "0" indicated neither like nor dislike.
All treatment options were elaborated on with a one sentence description, as well as a visual depiction.

text.text: We calculated means and standard deviations for each treatment option, as well as percentages of participants who "like" or "strongly like" each option as a metric of overall desire for a treatment option in a sample.
We ran one sample t-tests for each treatment option to calculate if the mean scores were significantly different from zero (neither like nor dislike).
We used a Holm-Bonferroni correction for the eight tests (Holm, 1979).
text.formatted: We used a Holm-Bonferroni correction for the eight tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Holm, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: We ran a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R that accounted for the by-subject random effects to assess the impact of treatment format (individual or group) and provider (DOC or peer) on preference for the four relevant options.

To account for the nonindependence in the data we included a by-subject random intercept in the model, so parameter estimates are unbiased leading to a reduction in type I and type II error rates (Brauer and Curtin, 2018).
text.formatted: To account for the nonindependence in the data we included a by-subject random intercept in the model, so parameter estimates are unbiased leading to a reduction in type I and type II error rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brauer and Curtin, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In the preregistration, we indicated that age, education level, and race would be included as covariates in the model.
However, when the model did not converge, it became clear that with a fully within-subjects design, between-subjects covariates are unnecessary.
The final model was: lmer(preference_score ~ provider*format (1 + provider*format|subID).

Three out of four incarcerated women experience mental health difficulties (James and Glaze, 2006), but research has rarely solicited feedback on their desired treatment options.

text.text: We surveyed incarcerated women about their mental health treatment preferences, presenting a variety of options that might appeal to different individuals and that could be feasibly implemented in prison.
A discussion of key findings and takeaways is presented below.
The desire for mental health treatment across the board is high.
At least 40% of individuals selected "like" or "strongly like" for every treatment option with 79% liking the most preferred option (self-help workbook).
Even the least preferred option (peer group support) was rated favorably by almost half of individuals.

The mean number of options rated favorably by each individual was 4.81, demonstrating discerning but broad interest in mental health treatments. 97% of participants liked or strongly liked at least one treatment option.
In a resource poor setting like a carceral facility, a "menu" of options could broaden access to vital mental healthcare.
In line with our hypothesis, self-administered treatment options were rated favorably by participants.
The self-help workbook (79%) and MP3 audio program (76%) were the two most preferred options.
Of those individuals who rated only one or two treatments favorably, the self-help workbook was the most desired option.

Self-administered mental health treatments have been shown to be effective (Cavanagh et al., 2014; K. J. Martin et al., 2018), and can provide a meaningful way to pass time during incarceration (Pederson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Self-administered mental health treatments have been shown to be effective <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cavanagh et al., 2014</ref>; K. J. <ref type="bibr">Martin et al., 2018)</ref>, and can provide a meaningful way to pass time during incarceration <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Pederson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Utilizing a self-administered intervention may be attractive for both incarcerated individuals because it affords privacy, continuity, and independence in the treatment process, and for correctional facilities by providing access to care for more individuals at a lower cost to staff time.
Contrary to our hypothesis, participants preferred treatment with a DOC provider to support from a peer provider.
Given prior research indicating mistrust for DOC psychiatric staff (Bright et al., 2022; Way et al., 2013), this result is surprising.
text.formatted: Given prior research indicating mistrust for DOC psychiatric staff <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bright et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Way et al., 2013)</ref>, this result is surprising.

text.text: Without qualitative data to understand the lower preference for peer support, we can use the literature on challenges related to peer support to provide context.
Research shows that peer support for mental health can create issues around boundaries, role conflict, and power (Miyamoto and Sono, 2012; Repper and Carter, 2011; Rodrik, 2024).
text.formatted: Research shows that peer support for mental health can create issues around boundaries, role conflict, and power <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Miyamoto and Sono, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Repper and Carter, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Rodrik, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The role as a peer provider allows disclosure of personal experiences to build rapport and trust with a patient.
However, this is atypical for a patientprovider relationship and the line between provider and friendship can lead to confusing relationship boundaries.

Certain obligations (such as reporting suicidal intent to the DOC) might become difficult to navigate for the peer provider and lead to a perceived breach of trust for the patient (Miyamoto and Sono, 2012).
text.formatted: Certain obligations (such as reporting suicidal intent to the DOC) might become difficult to navigate for the peer provider and lead to a perceived breach of trust for the patient <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Miyamoto and Sono, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Issues with power are also magnified in the prison environment (Repper and Carter, 2011).
text.formatted: Issues with power are also magnified in the prison environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Repper and Carter, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Peer providers are paid for their services by the DOC.
The payment, extensive training provided by the DOC, and the position title lead to power differentials.

It is possible that individuals who did not rate peer support favorably see the power differential with a peer in the prison environment as too threatening to both their physical and emotional safety.

In addition, there may be a need to interact with peers in settings outside of the support role (e.g., in dorm housing) which can cause distress around boundaries and confidentiality (DeHart and Mason, 2022).
text.formatted: In addition, there may be a need to interact with peers in settings outside of the support role (e.g., in dorm housing) which can cause distress around boundaries and confidentiality <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(DeHart and Mason, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Ultimately, while peer support is a viable option for those who are not sensitive to issues of boundaries, role conflict, and power differentials, it is not a universally preferred option.
That being said, peer support was rated favorably by a substantial portion of our sample and remains an important pathway to mental health support in the prison setting.
Our results also indicate that despite evidence for mistrust of DOC psychiatric staff, the desire for individual treatment from DOC remains high (72%).

In one mixed-methods study assessing mental health treatment needs of incarcerated women with history of intimate partner violence, participants expressed a demand and desire for individual therapy with trained clinicians (Lynch, Fritch, et al., 2012).
text.formatted: In one mixed-methods study assessing mental health treatment needs of incarcerated women with history of intimate partner violence, participants expressed a demand and desire for individual therapy with trained clinicians <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Lynch, Fritch, et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Another study with incarcerated men reported that individuals perceived prison psychologists as able to effectively assist with a range of emotional and mental health needs even with concerns about confidentiality and working within the "the system" (Skogstad et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Another study with incarcerated men reported that individuals perceived prison psychologists as able to effectively assist with a range of emotional and mental health needs even with concerns about confidentiality and working within the "the system" <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Skogstad et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals with previous contact with facility mental health staff had more positive attitudes about seeking help for mental health during incarceration (Skogstad et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Individuals with previous contact with facility mental health staff had more positive attitudes about seeking help for mental health during incarceration <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Skogstad et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Our results, along with prior empirical evidence presented here, suggest incarcerated individuals value educational credentials and training in their mental health providers and the exigency for treatment may override fears around confidentiality.
There was a strong preference for individual treatment and support options compared to group options, and this difference was larger for treatment with a DOC provider than with a peer.
This finding is importantly contextualized within the prison setting where group treatment and programming are more widely available.

While research shows that both group and individual interventions can be equally effective (Yoon et al., 2017), and that group therapy is seen favorably by incarcerated individuals (e.g., Zielenski et al., 2021; Doyle et al., 2022), patients may prioritize confidentiality, privacy, and individual processing over interpersonal connection in mental health treatment.
text.formatted: While research shows that both group and individual interventions can be equally effective <ref type="bibr">(Yoon et al., 2017)</ref>, and that group therapy is seen favorably by incarcerated individuals (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Zielenski et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Doyle et al., 2022)</ref>, patients may prioritize confidentiality, privacy, and individual processing over interpersonal connection in mental health treatment.

text.text: In addition, the one-day workshop (67%) was preferred to multi-session group options (DOC = 51%, peer = 42%).
It is possible that individuals are not ready to commit to treatment, but are still interested in learning more about mental health.
Given the greater availability of group options in this setting, it is also likely that previous experiences with groups in prison shaped participant responses.

Prior work with incarcerated women identified that incarcerated individuals view group treatments within prison as a "lecture" and desire more active discussion and engagement from DOC providers (Rodrik, 2024).
text.formatted: Prior work with incarcerated women identified that incarcerated individuals view group treatments within prison as a "lecture" and desire more active discussion and engagement from DOC providers <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Rodrik, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, lower group ratings could reflect either priorities for treatment, reflection on prior experiences, or both.

Lastly, our results mirror previous research that indicates mixed opinions about psychotropic medication use within incarcerated populations with half of the sample rating medication favorably (Casey and Bentley, 2017; Hassan et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Lastly, our results mirror previous research that indicates mixed opinions about psychotropic medication use within incarcerated populations with half of the sample rating medication favorably <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Casey and Bentley, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hassan et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Medication is viewed by both prison staff and incarcerated individuals as a viable option to reduce symptomatology and avoid mental health crises (Hassan et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Medication is viewed by both prison staff and incarcerated individuals as a viable option to reduce symptomatology and avoid mental health crises <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hassan et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Medication, when taken voluntarily, is an additional way incarcerated individuals can practice personal agency over their mental healthcare in an environment with strict limits on personal choice (Bentley and Casey, 2017).
text.formatted: Medication, when taken voluntarily, is an additional way incarcerated individuals can practice personal agency over their mental healthcare in an environment with strict limits on personal choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bentley and Casey, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: While medication is a desired approach by half of individuals, there is a sizable percentage who did not rate this option favorably.
Our findings provide guidance for mental health care best practices for individuals in prison settings based on feedback from the users of the services themselves.
Facilities can consider the following: 1) Confidentiality is key.

Multiple findings from this study (i.e., the dominance of selfadministered options and the preference for individual options over group options) point to the importance of confidentiality in mental health treatment for this population.
Therefore, clarity around the limits to confidentiality (e.g., threat to oneself or others) should be prioritized in all treatment formats and with both types of providers.
2) Invest in self-administered options.
While staff prioritize their efforts on crisis care, other lower-risk individuals who are still struggling with mental health can benefit from selfadministered options.
Self-administered treatments provide portability and continuity.

An individual may not be able to maintain regular appointments with the same group or therapist due to environmental factors outside the individual's control, such as release, transfer, lockdowns, court, restricted housing placement, changes in work schedule, staff shortages or turnover, etc.
Self-administered options can be continued despite these barriers.
In addition, selfhelp options can be utilized while an individual is on a waitlist for therapy.
With high mental health staff turnover and long waitlists to access prison-based programming (Pederson et al., 2024), self-administered options are a worthy investment.
text.formatted: With high mental health staff turnover and long waitlists to access prison-based programming <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Pederson et al., 2024)</ref>, self-administered options are a worthy investment.

text.text: 3) Incorporate individualized elements into group programming.
Seventy-two percent of individuals rated individual therapy with a DOC provider favorably.
While it may be infeasible to increase access to individual therapy with a DOC staff to this extent, correctional facilities can incorporate more individualized elements into group programming.
For example, if homework is assigned, allocate time to look over individuals' worksheets and answer clarifying questions.
Together with quick individual check-ins or expressions of care before and after groups, the attractiveness of group options may increase.
The high treatment ratings across the board as well as the favorability for both self-administered and the one-day workshop point to a desire for self-learning and self-work.

This mirrors previous research on correctional programming which indicates that individuals want to take advantage of offerings but limited availability, strict eligibility criteria, and long wait times cause frustration and a sense of alienation (Pederson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This mirrors previous research on correctional programming which indicates that individuals want to take advantage of offerings but limited availability, strict eligibility criteria, and long wait times cause frustration and a sense of alienation <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Pederson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: An opportunity such as a one-day workshop that appeals to many and can provide psychoeducational resources to a large group (ideally individuals keep resources after the workshop) can fill idle time and instigate the self-reflection process for those who have not yet engaged in mental health treatment.
At intake, mental health is typically assessed briefly to identify current high severity issues such as active psychosis, self-harm, suicidality, and substance withdrawal (M. S. Martin et al., 2018).
text.formatted: At intake, mental health is typically assessed briefly to identify current high severity issues such as active psychosis, self-harm, suicidality, and substance withdrawal (M. S. <ref type="bibr">Martin et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These screening tools are short and differentially sensitive at identifying mental health needs (Dietzel et al., 2017).
text.formatted: These screening tools are short and differentially sensitive at identifying mental health needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Dietzel et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Best practices include a second mental health screening stage after intake in order to triage those who require more detailed mental health assessment and intervention (Simpson and Forrester, 2018).
text.formatted: Best practices include a second mental health screening stage after intake in order to triage those who require more detailed mental health assessment and intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Simpson and Forrester, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: At this second mental health screening, a preference survey could assist with resource allocation.
Our survey was low burden to fill out at only eight questions and surveys can be customized to reflect the offerings of a particular facility.

DOC providers are more likely to choose a treatment option that the incarcerated individual will respond to clinically and reduce the risk of misallocating resources with information from a preference survey.

For instance, an individual who rates group therapy as "neutral" but self-help workbook as "strongly like" may take up a valuable group therapy spot from someone else who is more likely to benefit given their openness to the group.
If used during intake or screening, the purpose of the survey must be clearly articulated and ethically considered.
A preference survey should not be adopted to provide only one type of care.
For example, if an individual is interested in both medication and therapy or peer support, medication should not be the only strategy implemented.
Mental healthcare often requires a multi-pronged approach of both medication and psychotherapy.

While the current research is novel in that it is the first quantitative study to assess mental health treatment preferences in an incarcerated population, it is limited in a few notable ways that hinder generalizability and warrant further research.
First, we only assessed treatment preferences at a women's facility.
Incarcerated men and women present with different mental health profiles and pathways to their disorders.
Future research should also assess the specific preferences of incarcerated men.
Second, due to the recruitment procedures for the current research, our sample is not representative of the average population at a women's correctional facility.

Fifty-eight percent of the sample was screened for participation in a trauma treatment study before completing the survey, with at least 36% of the sample meeting criteria for PTSD (56 out of 90 recruited for the PTSD study; not assessed for the remaining 66 participants).
While the pathway to recruitment for the study was not random, the rates of PTSD are in line with the typical prevalence of PTSD for incarcerated women (Baranyi et al., 2018).
text.formatted: While the pathway to recruitment for the study was not random, the rates of PTSD are in line with the typical prevalence of PTSD for incarcerated women <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baranyi et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The exclusion of individuals with psychosis due to concerns around capacity to consent may have had a larger impact.
Up to 15% of individuals incarcerated at state prisons in the US experience psychotic symptoms (James and Glaze, 2006) and this population in particular has high mental health treatment needs.
text.formatted: Up to 15% of individuals incarcerated at state prisons in the US experience psychotic symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(James and Glaze, 2006)</ref> and this population in particular has high mental health treatment needs.

text.text: In addition, our sample underrepresented Black individuals and individuals with less than a high school education.

These individuals are historically excluded from mental health research (Spates, 2012; Steele et al., 2007) and their perspectives are needed to paint a fuller picture of treatment preferences for this population and to best inform clinical practice.
text.formatted: These individuals are historically excluded from mental health research <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Spates, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Steele et al., 2007)</ref> and their perspectives are needed to paint a fuller picture of treatment preferences for this population and to best inform clinical practice.

text.text: Finally, the absence of both qualitative data to supplement survey choices, as well as data on participants' prior experiences with mental health treatment while incarcerated, limited our ability to make conclusions about the "whys" behind individuals' ratings.

Future research should collect data on prior experience with each treatment option to parse apart true like or dislike for treatments from responses biased by the novelty of an option or prior experience.
In this study, we surveyed 156 individuals at a women's correctional facility about their mental health treatment preferences.
The results demonstrate a strong overall desire for a variety of mental health services, with a particular preference for self-administered options.
These data provide useful guidance on preferred mental healthcare options for incarcerated individuals.
